papers.title: Improving Prediction of Patient-Reported Health Outcomes Among Older Adults With Diabetes Across Diverse Populations Through Transfer Learning
papers.abstract: Population heterogeneity challenges the transportability of prediction models. Transfer learning may improve prediction through information borrowing, but its utility across population settings remains unclear. We evaluated a regression-based transfer learning framework across international aging cohorts (Gateway) and race/ethnicity groups within the RAND Health and Retirement Study (RAND HRS). Gateway included 19,879 adults with diabetes from eight cohorts, while RAND HRS included 3,926 participants across four race/ethnicity groups. Prediction models for patient-reported health outcomes were developed using demographic and clinical risk factors. Transfer learning was compared with target-only and pooled models using AUC and Brier score, with bootstrap resampling to assess uncertainty. Transfer learning improved prediction in 75% (6/8) of Gateway cohorts, with AUC gains of 0.1%-0.6%, and in all four RAND HRS race/ethnicity groups, with gains of 0.8%-3.1%. Improvements were greater and more consistent across within-cohort groups. These findings demonstrate the potential of regression-based transfer learning to improve prediction across heterogeneous populations. Information borrowing from sufficiently transferable external data may enhance prediction performance and provide meaningful public health benefits, even when improvements are modest, particularly in large population-based cohorts.

papers.title: Are time series foundation models the new frontier for operational epidemic forecasting?
papers.abstract: Time series foundation models (TSFMs) have emerged as a promising frontier in forecasting, particularly for their strong zero-shot performance (i.e., the ability to forecast without task-specific training) and domain generalization. Despite a few early studies, their potential for operational epidemic forecasting remains an open question. Here, we prospectively evaluate six state-of-the-art TSFMs (Chronos-2, Lag-Llama, Moirai-2, TabPFN-TS, TimeGPT, and TimesFM) for real-time short-term epidemic forecasting, providing each model with recent surveillance data. We benchmark their performance against that of individual and ensemble models submitted to FluSight and CovidHub, two U.S. CDC-coordinated collaborative hubs covering the U.S. national level and 52 U.S. jurisdictions. Forecasts were generated prospectively during the 2025/26 winter season for weekly laboratory-confirmed influenza or COVID-19 hospital admissions. Additionally, we conducted a retrospective evaluation of the 2024/25 season to assess the robustness of our findings. Our results show that TSFMs' performance is highly heterogeneous across diseases, locations, epidemic phases, and seasons. Among the TSFMs considered, Chronos-2, TimesFM, and TabPFN-TS are the most competitive; TimeGPT exhibits strong point-forecast accuracy but limited calibration; Moirai-2 shows context-dependent performance; and Lag-Llama consistently underperforms across all settings. Although the best-performing TSFMs achieve performance comparable to the multi-model ensemble in some forecasting instances, none does so consistently across diseases, locations, forecasting rounds, and evaluation metrics. The multi-model ensemble remains the most reliable strategy for communicating forecasts up to 3-weeks ahead to public health agencies and to the public. These findings highlight that TSFMs, despite promising performance, are not a single solution for epidemic forecasting, and that rigorous evaluation remains a prerequisite for their integration into operational forecasting efforts.

papers.title: COVID specificity of air pollution associations with mortality in Cook County Medical Examiner records
papers.abstract: Background: The double-hit hypothesis proposes that chronic fine particulate matter (PM2.5) exposure and acute nitrogen dioxide (NO2) exposure increase COVID-19 mortality. Spatially patterned pollution and mortality complicate interpretation of these associations. Objective: To test whether pollution exposure was more strongly associated with COVID deaths than with other natural deaths in Cook County Medical Examiner records. Methods: We linked death records with demographic characteristics, Census population data, and modeled and monitored pollution estimates. Adjusted logistic regression compared 10,887 COVID deaths with 4,123 contemporaneous non-COVID natural deaths during March 2020-August 2021; sensitivity analysis used 12,048 pre-pandemic non-COVID deaths. Population-weighted Monte Carlo analyses compared observed exposures with group-specific expectations. Separate spatial and temporal randomizations examined short-term NO2 exposure. Results: Higher five-year PM2.5 was associated with lower odds that a death record was classified as COVID rather than non-COVID (odds ratio per 1 microgram per cubic meter, 0.63; 95% confidence interval, 0.55-0.72), with a similar pre-pandemic comparison (0.54; 0.48-0.60). Modeled PM2.5 exceeded population-weighted expectations in both death groups. Modeled short-term NO2 excesses were small for COVID deaths and consistently larger for contemporaneous non-COVID deaths. At actual death times, NO2 exposure at death locations exceeded the population-weighted spatial expectation. At actual death locations, exposure immediately before death did not exceed the expectation based on randomized nearby times. Significance: Pollution associations in these records were not specific to COVID deaths. The NO2 comparisons supported a spatial interpretation without evidence of unusually elevated exposure immediately before death. The study does not estimate population-level mortality risk.

papers.title: The impact of adherence to the Australian social media ban on adolescents' psychological distress and daily functioning: an emulated trial
papers.abstract: Background. Australia was the first country to adopt a national minimum age requirement for social media use. This policy has been widely debated, and evidence is only just starting to emerge about its impacts on adolescents. This study examined the effect of the social media ban on psychological distress, health-related quality of life (HRQoL), and the impact on daily life and academic self-efficacy. Methods. We conducted an emulated trial using follow-up data collected three months after the ban implementation from a two-wave survey of South Australian high school students aged 12 to 15 (N=551). Exposure was defined as adherence to the ban, which was assessed in two ways: strictly (self-reported adherence combined with reported social media behaviours), and less strictly (self-report only). The primary outcome was the Revised Children's Anxiety and Depression Scale (RCADS-11). Secondary outcomes included RCADS-11 impact subscore; Child Health Utility 9 Dimensions (CHU9D) utility score (HRQoL); score of CHU9D activity-related items, which assessed daily functioning; and the academic self-efficacy subscale of the Self-Efficacy Questionnaire for Children (SEQ-C). Adjusted regression models were performed using inverse probability weighting to account for group imbalance and attrition. Findings. Using the strict definition, 14.8% of adolescents adhered to the ban, compared to 41.5% under the less stringent definition. Adherence had no significant effect on the RCADS-11 total score or impact subscore (p[≥].321). Those who adhered to the ban had significantly higher HRQoL, better daily functioning and higher academic self-efficacy (p[≤].033). Overall, effects were small in magnitude. No significant effects were observed under the less stringent definition of adherence (p=.244). Interpretation. Strict adherence to the social media ban was associated with minor short-term improvements in HRQoL and daily functioning, but not psychological distress. Funding. This research was supported by a Channel 7 Children's Research Foundation grant.

papers.title: Longitudinal changes of health-related quality of life, digital media use, and physical activity in children between 4-17 years during the COVID-19 pandemic in Germany
papers.abstract: Background: Evidence in youth on whether pandemic-related changes in physical activity (PA), recreational screen time (ST), and health-related quality of life (HRQoL) persisted after the COVID-19 pandemic is limited. In a longitudinal study, we examined changes from pre- to post-pandemic and whether these changes differed by age at pre-pandemic. Methods: Longitudinal data were obtained from 945 participants (49% female) aged 4-17 years pre-pandemic in the German Motorik-Modul Study. HRQoL, ST, everyday PA, and the number of days per week with at least 60 minutes of PA (WHO PA days) were assessed pre-pandemic (2018-2020), during both German lockdowns (2020 and 2021), and post-pandemic after restrictions ended (2023). Covariate-adjusted random-intercept mixed-effects models tested pre- to post-pandemic changes and moderation by baseline age. Lockdown trajectories were explored using successive contrasts. Results: Compared with pre-pandemic levels, post-pandemic HRQoL decreased (B = -5.92, 95% CI [-6.82, -5.03]), everyday PA decreased by 31.15 minutes per day (95% CI [-36.40, -25.91]), and WHO PA days decreased by 0.27 days per week (95% CI [-0.43, -0.11]). ST increased by 75.17 minutes per day (95% CI [66.65, 83.69]; all p < .001). Age moderated changes in HRQoL, ST, and everyday PA, but not WHO PA days. Children aged 6-13 years showed the greatest ST increases. Children younger than 11 years showed the largest everyday PA declines. Additionally explored trajectories varied across lockdowns and were moderated by age prior to the pandemic. Conclusions: Childrens and adolescents PA, ST, and HRQoL had not returned to pre-pandemic levels one year after COVID-19 restrictions were lifted. Developmentally tailored monitoring and interventions may be required, particularly for younger and school-aged children in face of ongoing global crises.

papers.title: Place or placeholder? AlphaEarth satellite embeddings did not detectably improve weekly dengue forecasts in four countries
papers.abstract: Background. Some recent disease forecasts use satellite embeddings (numbers summarising places). A model may use them only as a placeholder, recognising districts and their usual dengue levels without learning about the environment. We asked whether AlphaEarth embeddings improve weekly district dengue forecasts and whether gains go beyond such recognition. Methods. We retrospectively forecast cases one and four weeks ahead in 6,909 districts of Brazil, Colombia, Peru and Taiwan (OpenDengue, 2020-2024) with gradient boosting. In 14 comparisons across future years and held-out places, we measured how embeddings changed the weighted interval score, with and without a location control (an input that only identifies a district), to test whether location alone explains gains. We used Diebold-Mariano tests, the Holm correction and a +/-1% equivalence margin set after the first Brazil and Peru results. Findings. No comparison showed a significant gain after correction. Six showed losses: five small (-0.42% to -0.68%) and one with Taiwan held out (-18.3%; absolute -0.0037). Only Colombia's held-out-states loss (-0.52%) stayed significant under two stricter checks and a check for cases hidden in zero-filled weeks. In 8 comparisons (5 under the stricter checks), any gain or loss was shown to be smaller than 1% of forecast error. This margin is roughly Brazil's gain from all non-case inputs combined. In exploratory analyses, embeddings alone predicted district burden in unseen states. Without case history, neither coordinates nor embeddings helped detectably in Brazil's held-out states; both hurt in Colombia's. In Brazil's future years, coordinates cut error by 3.3% (1.7 to 4.9); embeddings added nothing detectable. Interpretation. Embeddings partly showed which districts usually have more dengue, but in Brazil and Colombia other non-case inputs already held most of it. With case history they added no detectable accuracy; without it, evidence was inconclusive. Embeddings should be tested against location-only controls in held-out places.

papers.title: Estimating the contribution of adults living with HIV to vaccine serotype pneumococcal transmission in Malawi after longstanding infant PCV13 vaccination
papers.abstract: Despite longstanding infant pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV13), residual vaccine-type (VT) carriage persists in Malawi, where human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) prevalence is high. Adults living with HIV (ALWH) on long-term (>1 year) antiretroviral therapy (ART) show higher pneumococcal carriage and shedding than HIV-uninfected adults, but their contribution to VT transmission remains unclear. We conducted a longitudinal household study in Malawi with weekly nasopharyngeal sampling and fitted a household transmission dynamic model using Markov Chain Monte Carlo methods. We collected 906 samples from 302 participants: younger children (0-5 years), older children (6-17 years) and adults (18+ years) stratified by HIV status and ART duration. VT transmission was more intense with household mixing, with ALWH on long-term ART contributing most to onward transmission to younger children. In contrast, non-vaccine serotype (NVT) transmission was driven mainly by younger children across multiple household pathways. Younger children and ALWH on long-term ART had prolonged carriage, which may have sustained household transmission. VT acquisition was driven mainly by household exposure, whereas NVT acquisition was balanced between household and community sources. Unvaccinated ALWH substantially contribute to household pneumococcal transmission, sustaining residual VT carriage. Optimal pneumococcal vaccination strategies targeting ALWH should be evaluated in high HIV prevalence low-income settings.

papers.title: Preparedness of health facilities for emergency neonatal care in West Cameroon: a cross-sectional study
papers.abstract: Background Limited access to quality emergency neonatal care (EmNC) contributes to high neonatal mortality in Cameroon, yet data on facility readiness in the West Region are scarce. This study assessed the preparedness of health facilities for EmNC in this region. Methods We conducted a cross-sectional study from March to May 2026 in five health districts of the West Region. All eligible facilities were included. Data were collected through a questionnaire for health professionals and an observation checklist adapted from the WHO/UNFPA SARA framework. Preparedness scores were classified as high ([≥]80%), moderate (60-79%) or low (<60%). Results We surveyed 185 health facilities (74.1% integrated health centers, 63.2% rural, 49.7% public) and 243 health professionals. The mean preparedness score was 51.1%; 11.4% of facilities had a high level of preparedness, 20.0% moderate and 68.6% low. At least one qualified staff member was present in 64.3% of facilities, and written neonatal protocols in 45.9%. Essential equipment was scarce: bag-valve-mask (13.0%), functional incubator (19.5%), newborn transport equipment (13.5%), phototherapy unit (10.8%) and defibrillator (7.6%), whereas vitamin K was widely available (95.7%). Mean scores were highest in private for-profit facilities (64.9%) compared with public (47.7%) and private non-profit facilities (45.1%), in district hospitals (66.2%) and CMAs (66.0%) compared with integrated health centers (45.9%), and in urban areas (60.9%) compared with rural (48.6%) and semi-urban areas (40.4%). Conclusions Most health facilities in the West Region are poorly prepared for newborn emergencies. Priorities include essential equipment with maintenance systems, qualified staff, written protocols and regular training, especially in integrated health centers and rural areas.

papers.title: Sources of protein in UK adults following contemporary plant-based diets: findings from the Feeding the Future (FEED) Study
papers.abstract: Objective To identify and quantify sources of protein intake in United Kingdom (UK) adults following different diets, and assess how these sources contribute to meeting protein requirements. Design Cross-sectional analysis of the Feeding the Future Study (FEED), a UK cohort recruited in 2022-2023. Dietary intake was assessed using an online food frequency questionnaire. We calculated the percentage contribution of food groups to daily protein intake, and the proportion of participants meeting the estimated average requirement (EAR) for protein, with and without exclusion of under-reporters. Setting A contemporary cohort of UK adults. Participants 6,113 adults: 1,540 omnivores, 1,322 flexitarians, 547 pescatarians, 1,212 vegetarians, and 1,492 vegans. Results Grains contributed 10-30% of total protein intake across all groups. Dairy contributed 12.9-14.2% in non-vegan groups, while plant-based dairy alternatives contributed less in vegans (7%), mainly from soy milk (4.3%). Other major contributors (>10%) were meat for omnivores (33.0%) and flexitarians (13.5%); fish for pescatarians (14.9%); plant-based meat alternatives for vegetarians (12.0%); and plant-based meat alternatives (15.0%), legumes and pulses (10.5%), and nuts and seeds (10.5%) for vegans. The proportion below the protein EAR ranged from 1.9% in omnivores to 14.0% in vegans, falling to 0.01% and 3.6% respectively, after excluding under-reporters. Conclusions Grains were a major contributor to protein intake across all diet groups, as was dairy in all non-vegan groups. Protein sources were more varied in non-omnivorous groups, particularly vegans. Few participants fell below the protein EAR and the higher proportions among vegetarians and vegans were largely attenuated after excluding under-reporters.

papers.title: Estimating timing of pre-emptive livestock vaccination to prevent human Rift Valley fever spillover in Rwanda: a modelling study
papers.abstract: Background Rift Valley fever recurred in Rwanda in 2018, 2022, 2025 and 2026 despite yearly livestock vaccination. Vaccines protect best if given before transmission speeds up, but the deadline for vaccination and the sectors to prioritise have not been estimated. We aimed to estimate the latest dates to start and finish a campaign and to identify priority sectors. Methodology We analysed surveillance data from four outbreaks: 1,090 animals and 416 laboratory-confirmed people in 2026, plus 2022, 2025 and 2018 data, vegetation and rainfall records. A negative binomial regression of weekly livestock cases gave the growth rate, the basic reproduction number and the start of transmission. We simulated the latest campaign dates 100,000 times, allowing for delays to immunity and campaigns. We ranked 416 sectors using pre-2026 information, tested by leaving out each district in turn. Livestock cases doubled every 9.3 days (95% confidence interval 8.1-10.8) and the basic reproduction number was 1.78 (1.64-1.92); assuming 90% vaccine efficacy, 48.5% coverage (43.4-53.3) was needed to stop spread. For the earliest outbreak (March 2022), live-attenuated vaccine had to start by 11 January (24 December-28 January) and finish by 22 February (11 February-3 March). A campaign begun at first detection would have protected animals after 220 of 1,090 livestock cases (20%) and 149 of 416 human cases (36%) had occurred. Sectors ranked before the season, mainly by the districts 2022 attack rate, that held 25% of animals contained 66% of livestock cases and 86% of human cases (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve 0.73). Conclusions Waiting until an outbreak is detected is too late to prevent many early cases, so campaigns should be planned around the earliest-starting outbreak, with a later round to protect animals through the year. Districts and sectors with earlier outbreaks should be prioritised.

papers.title: Disease-anchored organ aging clocks enable multi-organ risk profiling from routine labs
papers.abstract: Organ clocks estimate the biological age of organs from blood, but current clocks assign tissue-enriched proteins to organs and train on chronological age, which requires proteomics and does not yield organ-specific disease risk. In the UK Biobank, we trained organ clocks on first onset of disease of each organ using routine laboratory tests and froze the coefficients. Under an age label, organ-clock readouts arose equally in size-matched random protein panels; with a disease label, clocks selected their own organs proteins and predicted their own organs diseases. Defining extreme aging by multiples of disease risk concentrated flags on own-organ disease. Frozen clocks kept organ correspondence in the US NHANES cohort, predicted first onset of own-organ disease in the Japanese JMDC cohort and added more information to clinical risk scores than current organ clocks. Trained once where disease follow-up exists, organ clocks can be used wherever routine laboratory tests are measured.

papers.title: Distinguishing evidence of absence from absence of evidence in claims of safety: A methodological study with application to diagnostic hysteroscopy in endometrial cancer
papers.abstract: Background: Claims that an intervention is safe often rest on a nonsignificant difference, confusing absence of evidence with evidence of absence; an integrated, reproducible procedure for auditing them is lacking. We developed and evaluated one, applying it to diagnostic hysteroscopy in endometrial cancer, which published syntheses describe as oncologically safe. Methods and findings: The framework's eight steps verify each number, test the direction of confounding, require time-to-event analysis, bound detectability and apply one information-adjusted boundary to claims of harm and of safety (verdicts: harm established, safety established, inconclusive). The rule was fixed before a retrospective test on minimally invasive radical hysterectomy for cervical cancer, later assessed in a randomized trial, and evaluated analytically and by simulation. We audited 18 comparative studies of hysteroscopy, 12 with peritoneal cytology (4,078 patients) and 5 with time-to-event recurrence estimates. With a true hazard ratio (HR) of 1.25 and the information available for hysteroscopy, inferring safety from nonsignificance gave false reassurance in 34% of analyses and the rule in 1%; with adequate information and no harm, the rule established safety in 80%. Pre-trial evidence on minimally invasive radical hysterectomy proved inconclusive, not safe. For hysteroscopy, controlling for disease extent revealed an association with positive cytology (odds ratio 2.86, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.24-6.62) absent from crude comparisons; recurrence data (HR 1.17, Hartung-Knapp 95% CI 0.90-1.52) held 71% of the required information and were inconclusive at margins from 1.10 to 1.40; and harm through cytology would be undetectable in low-risk disease. Limitations include development on the case to which it is applied, a retrospective test of author-selected evidence, and reliance on published observational data. Conclusions: The framework distinguishes evidence of absence from absence of evidence in claims of safety and can be applied with a published confidence interval in minutes. It provides a reproducible, low-barrier procedure for clinicians, reviewers and guideline panels to audit such claims and apply proportionate precaution.

papers.title: Improving epidemic nowcasting with auxiliary information and geographic networks
papers.abstract: Monitoring infectious disease trends requires timely information on disease activity, but direct measurements suffer reporting delays, hindering public health response. Numerous less-direct measurements are collected rapidly, although their relationship to disease can change with behavior, reporting, and data availability. Here, we present GLCast, a statistical nowcasting framework that effectively uses auxiliary information to estimate delayed surveillance measurements, without requiring any verification beforehand that these data will improve performance. At each retraining window, GLCast automatically selects useful data streams through adaptive local regression and further learns dynamic epidemic neighbor graphs to aggregate models across. We evaluate GLCast on six years of weekly influenza-like illness with retail sales, three years of daily COVID-19 hospital admissions with search and survey signals, and seven recent influenza, COVID-19, and RSV surveillance targets with environmental, travel and online-attention streams. Against methods without auxiliary information, GLCast lowers mean prediction error by 25.1% for historical influenza-like illness and 12.9% for historical COVID-19 admissions against the strongest baselines, improving 45 of 45 and 49 of 51 evaluated jurisdictions, respectively, with further performance gains in critical upswing periods. In the seven modern targets, GLCast achieves the lowest overall error and maintains strong performance when multiple diseases experience overlapping upswings. Interpreting how GLCast uses additional information, we find that the features and neighbors selected are indeed dynamic over time and heterogeneous across different states. Interestingly, outbreaks appear to be change points where both feature and neighbor importance will dramatically shift. GLCast tends to assign new importance to auxiliary information at the peak of an outbreak, disregards neighbors during outbreaks, and heavily relies on neighbors during down periods. SignificancePublic health response depends on timely measures of disease activity, but direct surveillance reports often arrive late. Retail purchases, symptom searches, surveys, weather, and online attention offer earlier information whose usefulness changes across locations and epidemic phases. We introduce GLCast, a framework that repeatedly selects useful streams and learns which regional models can improve local estimates. Across nine applications, it improves nowcasting while revealing changing use of auxiliary information and geographic borrowing. Outbreaks are associated with shifts in stream importance, cross-state information is useful during down periods, and less useful during upswings. These interpretable outputs can help researchers identify promising surveillance signals and regional relationships.

papers.title: Intentional injuries in Ethiopia: the 2024/2025 Ethiopia Demographic and Health Survey
papers.abstract: Background Injuries and violence disproportionately affect disadvantaged populations, particularly males, young people and those living in low- and middle-income countries, where about 90% of injury-related deaths occur. Preventing injuries is integral to achieving several Sustainable Development Goals. This study aimed to assess the magnitude, characteristics, spatial distribution, and individual- and household-level determinants of intentional injuries in Ethiopia. Methods We analysed the 2024-25 Ethiopia Demographic and Health Survey, a two-stage stratified cluster survey of 21,241 households (97,262 members) in 797 geo-referenced clusters. Household respondents reported injuries among members in the preceding 12 months; injuries due to violence/assault, self-harm or conflict were classified as intentional. Survey-weighted rates per 100,000 were estimated. Spatial patterns were assessed with global Moran's I, Getis-Ord Gi* hotspot analysis and Kulldorff's Poisson scan statistic. Survey-weighted logistic regression compared intentional with unintentional non-traffic injuries (n = 222), and survey-weighted Poisson regression estimated household-level incidence rate ratios (IRRs). Results Of 435 injury events, 81 (18.6%) were intentional (38 conflict-related, 32 violence/assault, 11 self-harm), giving a weighted rate of 65.2 per 100,000 (95% CI 45.2-94.0) and a mortality rate of 14.6 per 100,000 (95% CI 7.5-28.3). Victims were mostly male (79.8%) and aged 15-29 years (51.0%), and gunshot was the commonest mechanism (36.7%). Intentional injuries were spatially clustered (Moran's I = 0.053, p = 0.004); all 74 hotspots were in Tigray, Amhara and Afar, with the primary scan cluster in Afar (RR = 19.7, p = 0.001) and a secondary cluster in Tigray and northern Amhara (RR = 3.6, p = 0.009). Self-harm showed no clustering. Male sex (AOR = 3.33; 95% CI 1.25-8.89) and age 15-29 (AOR = 4.40; 1.27-15.21) and 30-44 years (AOR = 5.53; 1.35-22.66) were associated with an injury being intentional. Households in the northern conflict-affected regions had a six-fold higher rate (adjusted IRR = 6.44; 95% CI 2.91-14.25). Conclusions About one in five household-reported injuries in Ethiopia was intentional. These injuries mainly affected young men, often involved firearms, and were concentrated in conflict-affected regions. Self-harm was probably under-reported. Conflict resolution, firearm control, and trauma and psychosocial services targeted at these hotspots, together with better surveillance of suicide and self-harm, are needed. Keywords: Intentional injury; Violence; Armed conflict; Self-harm; Spatial analysis; Demographic and Health Survey; Ethiopia

papers.title: Modelling the impact of a school-based influenza vaccination programme under uncertainty in seasonal transmission dynamics
papers.abstract: School-aged children are thought to be an important driver of influenza transmission. In this paper we study the direct and indirect health effects of a school-based live-attenuated influenza vaccination (LAIV) programme in Australia, using a stochastic, age-stratified model of seasonal influenza transmission. The model was calibrated using Approximate Bayesian Computation (ABC) in order to capture uncertainty in influenza infection dynamics. The calibrated model was used to evaluate programmes varying in target age group, vaccination coverage and vaccine effectiveness. On average, school-based LAIV programmes reduced infections and hospitalisations at the population level across all scenarios, with greater reductions at higher coverage and vaccine effectiveness and when both primary- and secondary-school-aged children were targeted. However, estimated effects varied substantially across plausible transmission dynamics, particularly indirect effects -- for some programme scenarios, we estimated that in non-target age groups both near complete suppression or a small increase in infections were possible outcomes. For all scenarios, we estimated that school-based LAIV programmes would lead to a reduction in infections and hospitalisations in target age groups.

papers.title: On the Distribution of Expected Case Reproductive Number in Compartmental Disease Models
papers.abstract: Heterogeneity in the expected number of secondary cases caused by infectors,[R] c, has long been characterized using a skewed distribution with mean[R] 0, typically under the assumption of a fully susceptible population. We have recently shown that over the entire course of an SIR-modeled outbreak, the variation in[R] c is constant and independent of[R] 0. Here, we extend that result by showing that the distribution of[R] c across infectors over the course of a canonical SIR epidemic is precisely the standard exponential distribution, corresponding to a mean-one geometric distribution of realized infections in the canonical stochastic version. This result is exact in the limit of a small initial infection, and also requires a long-time limit in the case of persistent outbreaks. This result also applies to extensions of the model that allow immune waning and changes in[R] 0 across time (or as a function of susceptible density), but only if the infectious period remains exponentially distributed. The distribution of[R] c, varies with[R] 0 when the generation-interval distribution is not exponential. Our findings highlight the critical role of the infectious period distribution in shaping the long-term outcomes of an outbreak.

papers.title: Productivity-adjusted life years lost due to type 2 diabetes by socioeconomic position in Germany between 2022 and 2060
papers.abstract: Introduction: Type 2 diabetes can impair productivity during working age (20-69 years), causing substantial economic burden at individual and at population level. We aimed to estimate age- and sex-specific productivity-adjusted life years (PALYs) lost due to type 2 diabetes by socioeconomic position (SEP) between 2022 and 2060 in Germany. Methods: We used an established projection model and nationally representative, publicly available German data to estimate age- and sex-specific PALYs lost due to type 2 diabetes by SEP among working-age adults, accounting for future incidence trends. PALYs lost were calculated as the sum of years of life lost (YLL) and years of productivity lost (YPL) due to reduced labour force participation, presenteeism, and absenteeism, using SEP-specific estimates from representative studies. Results: Productivity losses were highest among persons with low SEP, followed by those with medium and high SEP. In 2022, 20-year-old men with type 2 diabetes and low, medium, and high SEP were projected to lose 11.32 PALYs (95% confidence interval (CI) 7.99-14.56), 8.19 PALYs (95% CI 6.01-10.33), and 3.78 PALYs (95% CI 0.89-6.72), respectively, by age 69 compared with men without type 2 diabetes, mainly driven by YPL. A comparable socioeconomic gradient was observed among women and remained largely unchanged until 2060. At the population level, an estimated 9.5 million PALYs (95% CI 6.42-12.58) were lost due to type 2 diabetes in 2022 in both sexes. This number is projected to increase to 9.5-13.5 million by 2060, mainly driven by the projected increase in the number of persons with type 2 diabetes. Conclusion: Type 2 diabetes-related productivity losses were shaped by SEP, sex and the future number of persons with the disease. PALYs lost declined with age and were predominantly driven by YPL.

papers.title: Meta-analysis of Sequencing Data Identifies Candidate Endometrial Cancer Susceptibility Genes
papers.abstract: BackgroundEndometrial cancer is the most common gynaecological malignancy in high-income countries, yet its genetic architecture remains incompletely understood. While pathogenic variants in mismatch repair genes are well-established contributors, the role of rare variants in other genes has not been systematically characterized. MethodsWe evaluated associations between rare genetic variants and endometrial cancer risk based on 2,675 cases and 160,654 controls from the UK Biobank and the 100,000 Genomes Project. Gene-level associations were assessed using burden tests, with protein-truncating variants (PTVs) and missense variants (MSVs) predicted to be deleterious analysed separately. ResultsEndometrial cancer (EC) risk associations were observed for three established EC susceptibility genes in the rare PTV analysis: MSH6 (RR = 36.6, 95% CI 25.9-51.8), MLH1 (RR = 52.5, 95% CI 21.3-129.4) and MSH2 (RR = 13.0, 95% CI 6.0-28.2). In the rare MSV analysis, PTEN was also significantly associated with EC risk (RR = 9.7, 95% CI 4.0-23.7). Beyond these established susceptibility genes, exome-wide significance was observed for 19 additional genes in the PTV analysis, including PHKG2 (RR = 29.8, 95% CI 9.6-92.8), and eight additional genes in the MSV analysis. ConclusionThis study identifies novel candidate genes associated with endometrial cancer risk, providing a foundation for future replication studies.

papers.title: Missing Outcomes and Treatment Effect Estimates in the A4 Study of Solanezumab
papers.abstract: INTRODUCTIONMissing final-visit outcome measurements may bias treatment effect estimates in amyloid-targeting drug trials. We examined whether accounting for missing Week-240 outcomes changed estimated treatment differences in the Anti-Amyloid Treatment in Asymptomatic Alzheimers Disease (A4) trial. METHODSWe reanalyzed 1,169 randomized participants, assessing baseline-to-Week-240 change in amyloid positron emission tomography (PET) Centiloids, the Preclinical Alzheimer Cognitive Composite (PACC), and Clinical Dementia Rating-Sum of Boxes (CDR-SB). We compared available-case estimates with inverse probability of censoring weighting (IPCW; primary analysis) and multiple imputation under missing at random (MAR), and assessed departures from MAR with delta-adjusted missing not at random (MNAR) analyses. RESULTSWeek-240 amyloid PET, PACC, and CDR-SB were missing for 352 (30.1%), 345 (29.5%), and 343 (29.3%) participants. IPCW treatment differences (solanezumab minus placebo) were -8.74 Centiloids (95% bootstrap CI, -11.75 to -5.86), -0.076 PACC points (CI, -0.691 to 0.517), and 0.126 CDR-SB points (CI, -0.077 to 0.320). These were close to the available-case differences of -8.56 Centiloids, -0.100 PACC points, and 0.120 CDR-SB points, and the MAR imputation differences. Assuming missing solanezumab outcomes were 0.50 SD worse than MAR predictions, differences were -3.48 Centiloids (95% CI, -6.50 to -0.46), -0.981 PACC points (CI, -1.602 to -0.360), and 0.297 CDR-SB points (CI, 0.112 to 0.481). DISCUSSIONMethods assuming that missingness is explained by measured data did not change the A4 findings. The amyloid result withstood large departures from this assumption, but PACC and CDR-SB results became unfavorable under modest ones, so conclusions for these outcomes depend on why data are missing.

papers.title: Personal HbA1c trajectories and incident diabetes: association, prediction and observability in the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing
papers.abstract: BackgroundClinical diagnosis often relies on a snapshot: a single measurement interpreted against a population threshold. Repeated (longitudinal) measurements, however, may reveal an individuals typical level and how it changes over time. Extracting this information is challenging when measurements are sparse and biological fluctuations may resemble sustained changes. Using data from the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing (ELSA), we investigated whether individual glycated haemoglobin (HbA1c) trajectories improved the prediction of incident diabetes beyond the most recent measurement, whether they were associated with incident diabetes, and how reliably they could be estimated. MethodsIn this secondary analysis of a prospective cohort study, we analysed venous HbA1c measured approximately every four years in ELSA, with a longer final interval of about seven years. A linear mixed model estimated each persons usual HbA1c level and rate of change (personal slope) from their measurements before each diabetes-free health visit, with model parameters estimated in other participants (cross-fitting). We derived four longitudinal features: deviation from the persons usual level, personal slope, change since the last measurement, and the forecast probability that the next HbA1c reaches the diagnostic threshold for diabetes. We evaluated the associations of these features with incident diabetes and their incremental predictive value beyond baseline HbA1c and clinical risk factors in internal, cross-fitted validation, compared predictive performance with a self-supervised Transformer, and modelled within-person variation as serially correlated drift (an Ornstein- Uhlenbeck process) to assess how reliably personal slopes can be recovered under different measurement schedules. ResultsThe analysis included 5,828 diabetes-free baseline visits from 3,603 participants, of which 234 were followed by incident diabetes. Neither the engineered longitudinal features nor a Transformer that also used additional clinical variables improved discrimination beyond baseline HbA1c and clinical risk factors (difference in the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve, {Delta}AUC, -0.002 to +0.010; all 95% confidence intervals [CIs] including zero). The estimated personal slope was nevertheless associated with incident diabetes after adjustment for baseline HbA1c, age and other clinical factors (odds ratio [OR] per standard deviation [SD] 1.18, 95% CI 1.02-1.36, and 1.39, 1.11-1.74, among visits with at least two earlier HbA1c values), whereas deviation from the persons usual level was not (OR 0.99, 95% CI 0.81-1.21). In the drift model, serially correlated fluctuations accounted for 77-81% of residual within-person variance, although the estimated temporal structure was sensitive to the treatment of the first HbA1c values at or above the diagnostic threshold. Under this model, persistent individual trends were difficult to distinguish from slowly varying fluctuations: with the intercept-slope correlation set to zero, estimated and underlying slopes correlated weakly for four-yearly measurements over up to 12 years (r [≤] 0.26), and more frequent measurements improved this little. ConclusionsEstimated personal HbA1c slopes carried adjusted prognostic information beyond baseline HbA1c and clinical factors, but longitudinal features, including those learned by a Transformer, did not clearly improve prediction. The drift model suggests that slowly varying within-person fluctuations may limit the reliable estimation of individual slopes from sparse measurements, and that longer observation histories are more informative than more frequent measurement. Whether personal laboratory histories improve prediction depends not only on their association with disease, but also on how reliably individual change can be recovered from the available measurements.

papers.title: Incidence of and Patient-Reported Reasons for Transfer-Out Among People Receiving Long-Acting Antiretroviral Therapy in Ndola District, Zambia: A Multisite Cross-Sectional Study of Formal and Silent Transfers
papers.abstract: Abstract Background. Transfer-out is a common outcome in HIV treatment programmes, and transfers that are not documented ("silent transfers") are often misclassified as loss to follow up. Understanding why recipients of care move between facilities, and which reasons lead to undocumented moves, can guide retention strategies. We estimated the incidence of transfer-out and described patient-reported reasons for formal and silent transfer among people receiving antiretroviral therapy (ART) in Ndola District, Zambia. Methods. We conducted a cross-sectional study in 11 ART facilities between April and October 2026. All recipients of care who transferred during the study period and consented were interviewed using a World Health Organization (WHO)-adapted questionnaire: formal transfers at exit and silent transfers by telephone once re-engagement elsewhere was established. Reasons were coded into structural, psychosocial and clinic-based domains. We report proportions with Wilson 95% confidence intervals (CIs) and used Firth penalized logistic regression to identify factors associated with silent rather than formal transfer. Results. Of 9,866 recipients of care on ART, 120 transferred out (cumulative incidence 1.22%; 95% CI 1.02-1.45%). The median age was 41 years (IQR 32-48.5) and 61.3% were female; 12 (10.0%) were silent transfers. Structural reasons accounted for 90.8% (95% CI 84.3-94.8) of transfers: work, education or business (55.0%), relocation (32.5%) and distance or transport (3.3%). Psychosocial reasons (marriage or family obligations) accounted for 9.2% (95% CI 5.2-15.7), and no participant reported a clinic-based reason. Silent transfer was more frequent among those reporting psychosocial than structural reasons (45.5% vs 6.4%; adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 11.36 (2.75-49.56)). Silent transfers were younger than formal transfers (median 33 vs 41 years; P = 0.031), while sex was not associated with transfer type. Conclusions. Transfer-out in Ndola District was uncommon and driven almost entirely by mobility linked to work and relocation rather than dissatisfaction with care. Transfers prompted by marriage or family obligations were much more likely to be undocumented. Asking recipients of care about upcoming life changes, offering facilitated transfers, and using a shared electronic health record could keep mobile recipients of care visible in the HIV programme.

papers.title: Heterogeneity in excess respiratory acute care utilization during wildfire smoke waves in California
papers.abstract: RationaleWildfire smoke is an increasing public health threat, yet most epidemiologic studies estimate average smoke-health associations across broad spatial or temporal scales. Such approaches may obscure substantial heterogeneity across individual smoke waves, leaving an important evidence gap for dynamic public health preparedness, risk communication, and clinical practice. ObjectivesTo estimate event-specific excess respiratory acute care utilization during smoke waves and identify smoke wave features associated with higher excess utilization. MethodsWe conducted a statewide study of 18,271,754 respiratory acute care encounters in California from 2006 to 2019. A smoke wave was defined as at least 2 consecutive days during which county-level wildfire smoke fine particulate matter (PM2.5) exceeded the 95th percentile over the study period. We applied a machine learning-integrated two-stage interrupted time-series design to estimate excess respiratory acute care utilization during each event. We then used meta-regressions to examine multiple spatiotemporally varying effect modifiers such as smoke wave duration, intensity, timing, and co-occurring climate and meteorological conditions. Measurements and Main ResultsA total of 1,249 smoke waves were identified and examined in this study. Excess respiratory acute care utilization varied substantially across smoke waves. Higher excess utilization was associated with longer smoke wave duration, greater intensity, winter occurrence, short recovery period, overlap with holidays, drought conditions, or co-occurrence with precipitation or extreme heat events. ConclusionsThis study proposes a novel analytical framework to systematically evaluate spatiotemporal drivers of heterogeneity in wildfire smoke respiratory health effects. The findings can inform dynamic preparedness and public health response to smoke events.

papers.title: Tuberculosis Severity metrics poorly predict Two-Month Culture Conversion
papers.abstract: ObjectivesAmong people with pulmonary tuberculosis (PTB), culture conversion (bacterial clearance) after two months of treatment is a critical indicator of response. However, predictors of culture conversion at two months are difficult to define and can be context specific. In this study, we evaluated how well two tuberculosis (TB) severity metrics, the chest Xray (CXR) Score and the Bandim TBScore associate with and predict two-month culture conversion. MethodsThe cohort contained 718 index PTB cases enrolled in "The Kawempe Community Health Study (KCHS)". We analyzed severity metrics, demographics, clinical, microbiological, radiological, household and behavioral data for their association with and their ability to predict culture conversion. ResultsSixty-eight percent of participants culture converted at two months. The highest CXR Score category (odds ratio (OR) 0.51, 95% Confidence Interval (CI) 0.31, 0.84), smear grade at diagnosis (OR 0.42, 95% CI; 0.26, 0.62), pleural thickening (OR 0.41, 95% CI 0.17, 0.95) and current smoking (OR 0.31, 95% CI 0.09, 0.99) inversely associated with conversion. Both severity measures and the most parsimonious model poorly predicted culture conversion (all AUCs<0.70). ConclusionCXR Score, higher smear grade at diagnosis, pleural thickening, and current smoking inversely associated with culture conversion but provided limited utility for prediction.

papers.title: Environmental Chemical and Psychosocial Stress Exposures during Pregnancy and Child Behavioral Problems through 10 Years of Age in a South African Birth Cohort
papers.abstract: IntroductionPrenatal exposure to environmental chemicals and psychosocial stress often co-occur in low- and middle-income settings, yet their joint effects on child behavior from preschool to school-age remain unknown. We investigated the joint associations of prenatal chemical metabolites and psychosocial stress on child behavior in the first decade of life in the South African birth cohort, the Drakenstein Child Health Study. MethodsAmong 643 mother-child pairs, we quantified 25 chemical metabolites spanning nine classes (organophosphates, pyrethroids, neonicotinoid, chlorinated phenol, polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, parabens, bisphenols, UV filters, other biocides) in second-trimester maternal urine and characterized prenatal psychosocial stress as a five-indicator latent construct using confirmatory factor analysis. Internalizing and externalizing problems were assessed with the Child Behavior Checklist (CBCL) at 2, 3.5, 5, 6.5, 8, and 10 years. We fit adjusted generalized estimating equations for single exposures with false discovery rate correction. We assessed the joint effects of the positively associated exposure classes using quantile-based g-computation (QG-COMP). Models were fit separately in the preschool (2 to 5 years) and school-age (6.5 to 10 years) developmental windows. Finally, we tested effect measure modification by maternal psychosocial stress and by child sex. ResultsChemical associations were confined to the preschool window. Three polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon (PAH) metabolites were associated with increased externalizing problems (2-hydroxyfluorene 1.49 [95% CI 0.37, 2.60]; 1-naphthol 1.14 [0.21, 2.07]; 1-hydroxypyrene 1.05 [0.14, 1.95]), as was the PAH mixture (externalizing {psi}=1.00 [0.32, 1.68]; internalizing {psi}=0.95 [0.26, 1.64]). Psychosocial associations persisted across both windows (e.g. latent stress score and externalizing problems: 1.52 [0.83, 2.22] preschool, 1.45 [0.77, 2.14] school-age). The joint PAH and psychosocial mixture showed the largest effects at preschool (externalizing {psi}=2.15 [1.15, 3.15]; internalizing {psi}=2.02 [0.98, 3.06]), with psychosocial factors contributing most to the joint effect. Preschool associations were present among boys, but not girls (joint mixture, externalizing: {psi}=3.42 [2.09, 4.69] in boys versus 0.74 [-0.67, 2.14] in girls, interaction p=0.004). There was no evidence of modification by maternal psychosocial stress. DiscussionPrenatal urinary PAH metabolite levels and psychosocial exposures were associated with child behavioral problems through distinct developmental courses, with PAH associations limited to early childhood and psychosocial associations persisting into the school-age years. Their joint effect exceeded that of either domain alone, and was heightened among boys during the preschool years. These findings highlight the importance of joint chemical and non-chemical stressors on child mental health.

papers.title: DYCAST early warning system for dengue virus risk areas, Ribeirao Preto, Brazil
papers.abstract: Dengue is currently the fastest-spreading vector-borne disease, with an estimated 100-400 million infections per year and nearly 6 billion people at risk - more than half the worlds population. However, there is no specific antiviral treatment, thus the primary method for preventing infection is through targeted control of the principal mosquito vector, Aedes aegypti. The objective of this retrospective study is to evaluate the efficacy of forecasting dengue risk using human cases and an adaptation of DYCAST: a biologically based, spatiotemporal clustering model that proved operationally successful as a West Nile virus early warning system. Results demonstrate that DYCAST provided accurate and early detection of high-risk areas for dengue in Ribeirao Preto, Brazil, including a cryptic interepidemic focus of transmission preceding a severe epidemic. Using suspected cases, DYCAST predicted 90.3% (4,237/4,690) of confirmed cases, with a mean lead time of 66.3 days prior to illness onset. High-risk cells had >10x higher relative risk of containing a confirmed case, and sensitivity and specificity were 83.8% and 72.3%. These findings suggest that DYCAST could be utilized in real time to prospectively identify areas at high risk of dengue, for rapid and precise targeting of mosquito mitigation and public education. Implementation using free, open-source software offers a scalable technological strategy for the prevention and control of dengue around the world. This article is part of the theme issue The Dengue Prevention Toolbox: Integrating Biological, Social and Technological Strategies for Sustainable Control.

papers.title: Epidemiology of Cardiac Structure and Function Among African Caribbeans in Tobago: A Population-based Cohort Study
papers.abstract: BackgroundIndividuals of African genetic ancestry are at high risk for heart failure (HF), which is often preceded by cardiac structural and functional abnormalities. Nevertheless, little is known about cardiac structure and function among Afro-Caribbeans residing in Tobago. This study aimed to investigate the epidemiology of cardiac structure and function among African Caribbeans in Tobago. MethodsA total of 924 participants (41-83 years) underwent clinical evaluation and transthoracic echocardiography. Images were analyzed for left ventricular (LV) mass index (MI), left atrial volume index, diastolic dysfunction (DD), LV ejection fraction (LVEF), global longitudinal strain (GLS), E/e' ratio, E/A ratio, and other echocardiographic measures. Cardiac structure and function were evaluated by age, sex, and HF stage. ResultsThe mean age was 61.7 years, with 61.4% women, 47.8% obesity, and 20.2% diabetes. Average systolic blood pressure was approximately 140 mmHg, and 76.7% had hypertension. Abnormal LV geometry was present in 77.1% of participants, predominantly concentric remodeling (69.5%). The prevalence of DD was 13.4%, LVEF <50% was 1.5%, and abnormal GLS ([≤]-18%) was 5.2%. Women had significantly higher E/e' ratios and a higher prevalence of Stage A and Stage B HF, whereas men had a higher prevalence of symptomatic (Stage C) HF. Participants aged 65-83 years had significantly higher E/e' ratio, concentric remodeling, and LV hypertrophy than those aged 41-57 years. ConclusionsWomen and older adults have higher LV structural abnormalities and DD than men and younger adults. These results will be helpful to inform public health priorities related to cardiovascular health in Tobago.

papers.title: Depressive Symptom Trajectories and Incident Cognitive Impairment by Outcome Ascertainment
papers.abstract: ImportanceDementia prevention frameworks treat depression as a leading modifiable risk factor, but cohort estimates of the association vary widely; whether this variation reflects how cognitive outcomes are ascertained is unknown. ObjectiveTo examine whether associations between depressive symptom trajectories and incident cognitive impairment vary by outcome ascertainment rigor. Design, Setting, and ParticipantsThis harmonized cohort study included 91,043 adults aged 50 years or older from 4 national longitudinal aging cohorts (CHARLS [China], HRS [US], ELSA [England], and SHARE [16 European countries]); baseline waves spanned 2006 to 2011, with follow-up through 2023. ExposureDepressive symptom trajectory classes (persistent low, persistent high, incident worsening, remitting) derived using group-based trajectory modeling. Main Outcomes and MeasuresIncident cognitive impairment ascertained under a 5-level hierarchy of increasing rigor, from self-report (level 1) to clinical consensus diagnosis (level 5; Harmonized Cognitive Assessment Protocol [HCAP]). Cohort-specific Cox models were pooled by random-effects meta-analysis; meta-regression tested ascertainment rigor as a moderator of heterogeneity. ResultsUnder nonadjudicated outcomes, the incident-worsening trajectory was associated with incident cognitive impairment in CHARLS (HR, 1.31; 95% CI, 1.06-1.62) and SHARE (HR, 1.99; 95% CI, 1.87-2.13) but not HRS (HR, 1.05; 95% CI, 0.95-1.16) or ELSA (HR, 1.10; 95% CI, 0.95-1.27); the persistent-high trajectory was not significant under any nonadjudicated outcome (HR range, 1.07-1.15). Under clinical consensus diagnosis (n = 3,196), all non-low trajectories were independently associated with mild cognitive impairment or dementia (OR range, 1.66-2.29; dementia-only persistent high: OR, 3.32; 95% CI, 1.85-5.95). Effect sizes increased stepwise with ascertainment rigor (meta-regression slope, 0.314 log HR per level; P < .001; residual I2 = 0%; R2 = 100%; exploratory). Findings were robust to lagged, weighted, and competing-risk analyses; biological aging acceleration did not differ across trajectories. Conclusions and RelevanceThe detectability and magnitude of depression-related cognitive risk depend on outcome ascertainment rigor. Prevention trials and burden projections relying on self-reported outcomes may underestimate the benefit of depression treatment. Key PointsO_ST_ABSQuestionC_ST_ABSDo associations between depressive symptom trajectories and incident cognitive impairment vary by the rigor of outcome ascertainment? FindingsIn this cohort study of 91,043 adults from 4 international cohorts, effect sizes increased stepwise across a 5-level outcome ascertainment hierarchy. Only incident-worsening trajectories were detectable under nonadjudicated outcomes, while clinical consensus diagnosis revealed independent associations for all non-low trajectories (ORs, 1.66-2.29). MeaningPrevention trials and burden projections that rely on self-reported outcomes may underestimate the potential benefit of treating depression.

papers.title: Elevated maternal hemoglobin levels during pregnancy are associated with autism spectrum disorder in the offspring: A population-based cohort study
papers.abstract: BackgroundAutism spectrum disorder (ASD) is an increasingly prevalent neurodevelopmental condition with multifactorial origins, including potential prenatal environmental contributions. Maternal anemia (decreased hemoglobin [Hb] levels) has long been associated with adverse offspring neurodevelopmental outcomes, yet evidence regarding elevated levels of antenatal hemoglobin levels, in relation to ASD risk remains limited. This study evaluated the association between maternal Hb levels during pregnancy and the risk of ASD diagnosis in offspring. MethodsThis large-scale, population-based retrospective cohort study used electronic health records from births of members of Clalit Health Services (CHS), the largest health maintenance organization in Israel, between 2011 and 2021. The study included 303,234 singleton live births to Jewish mothers who had at least one measured prenatal Hb value and were CHS members. Exclusion criteria were children with known genetic disorders and births 97.5th percentile). The main outcome was a diagnosis of ASD in the offspring, as recorded in medical files. Statistical analyses adjusted for maternal age, socioeconomic status, gestational diabetes, BMI, and other clinical and demographic factors. ResultsAmong the 303,234 births, 8,106 (2.7%) children were diagnosed with ASD. High maternal Hb levels were associated with elevated odds of ASD diagnosis (aOR=1.22; 95% CI=1.08-1.37), with the strongest association observed for first-trimester measurements (aOR=1.31; 95% CI=1.14-1.49). This association persisted in the sibling-matched analysis (aOR=1.64; 95% CI=1.08-2.47) and was not modified by maternal RBC levels, suggesting that it was not explained by familial factors or RBC counts. The main limitations of this study include the lack of available data on maternal smoking, and the absence of detailed information on maternal nutritional status. ConclusionsThese findings suggest that elevated antenatal Hb levels may be relevant to offspring neurodevelopment. Further studies are needed to replicate these findings and clarify the biological mechanisms underlying this association.

papers.title: Chronic Maternal White Blood Cell Elevation During Pregnancy and Offspring Autism
papers.abstract: BackgroundMaternal immune activation is a robust risk factor for autism spectrum disorder (ASD). Current evidence relies on specialized immunological markers not routinely measured, limiting population-level risk identification. We investigated the association between maternal white blood cell (WBC) counts, a ubiquitous component of routine prenatal care during pregnancy, and offspring ASD risk. MethodsWe conducted a retrospective population-based cohort study of 303,234 singleton live births (51% male) between 2011 and 2021 from Clalit Health Services in Israel. Exposures were maternal total and differential WBC counts from routine testing during the 1st and 2nd trimesters. High and low exposures were defined as >97.5th and <2.5th percentiles, respectively. The primary outcome was clinical ASD diagnosis. Analyses included multivariable logistic regressions, matched-sibling analyses (n=2,894 discordant pairs), and chronicity analyses in multiparous mothers (n=72,102). ResultsAmong 303,234 children, 8,106 (2.7%) were diagnosed with ASD. Elevated maternal total WBC counts were associated with increased odds of ASD (adjusted odds ratio [aOR]=1.59; 95% CI, 1.43-1.75), with the strongest association in the 1st trimester (aOR=1.64; 95% CI, 1.45-1.85). Similar associations were seen with elevated neutrophils, lymphocytes, and monocytes. While most associations were attenuated in matched-sibling analyses, chronicity analysis revealed increased ASD odds in offspring of mothers with persistently elevated WBC counts across multiple pregnancies (aOR=1.49; 95% CI, 1.08-2.01). ConclusionsPersistently elevated maternal WBC counts across pregnancies are associated with increased offspring ASD risk. These routinely collected hematologic markers support the maternal immune activation hypothesis and may contribute to future prenatal risk assessment models.

papers.title: The health and wellbeing impact of arts engagement: A longitudinal outcome-wide approach in 22 countries
papers.abstract: Arts and cultural engagement is increasingly recognised as a potential resource for health and wellbeing, yet evidence remains dominated by Western, high-income countries. Using data from the Global Flourishing Study across 22 countries (N=118,045), we examined associations between arts engagement and 19 health and wellbeing outcomes across five domains, applying an outcome-wide analytical framework and random-effects meta-analysis. Arts engagement was consistently associated with greater positive wellbeing and character strengths, higher evaluative wellbeing, and better social and general health, including lower loneliness. By contrast, associations with future-oriented wellbeing and perceived capability were less robust, and no pooled associations emerged for psychological distress. Country-level characteristics explained little cross-national variation. These findings suggest that arts engagement may promote flourishing across diverse cultural contexts, with benefits extending beyond the prevention of psychological distress, highlighting its potential role as a global population health resource.
